cues.text: A heart is placed on a scale.

On the other side sits a symbol of what is
right and true.

Standing beside the scale is a god with
the head of a canine: Anubis.

He is famous as the fearsome judge of the
dead.

But look closely at the ancient sources,
and you will find that Anubis does not
judge alone.
So what was Anubis actually doing?

Watching over tombs, protecting the bodies
of the dead, guiding them on their

journey, and checking the scale that
weighs the heart.

In this episode, we follow sculptures and
papyri at The Metropolitan Museum of Art

to see, one by one, the work Anubis does
in the sources.

On screen you will see photographs of real
museum objects, along with reconstructions
created to help you picture the past.

Every reconstruction is labeled in the top
corner.
Let's begin with the first object.
First, this statue of a reclining canine.

Its front legs stretch forward and its
ears stand upright.

It seems less asleep than alert, keeping
watch.

This statue at the Met is carved from
limestone and was originally painted
black.

The god was not always shown in human
form.

The museum's description draws attention
to the link between canines and
cemeteries.

Animals that roamed burial grounds could
disturb the dead.

Yet a watchful canine could also be
imagined as a power that guarded them.

This is an interpretation of the image's
background, not proof of a single origin
for Anubis.

In another statuette, an animal head sits
on a human body.

It is made of wood, and fine details of
the clothing still survive.

The museum describes it as probably
Anubis, because more than one god was
shown with a canine head.

A familiar look does not always tell us
the name for certain.
This is where dates matter.

The statues we have just seen and the
royal relief we will see later were not
made in the same era.

Ancient Egypt covers an enormous span of
time.

To understand a god's form and role, we
need to ask not only what is depicted, but
when the object was made.

One of Anubis's most important roles was
his connection to mummification.

In ancient belief, preparing the body of
the deceased and performing rituals helped
sustain their existence after death.

Preserving the body was not only about
appearance.
It was tied to the hope of living again.

A gilded coffin made for a priest named
Nedjemankh was once displayed at the Met.

The museum's description points to a scene
of a mummy on a bier, with Anubis
performing rites beside it.

Isis and Nephthys also appear as
protectors of the mummy.

The coffin was later found to have been
looted, and in 2019 it was returned to
Egypt.

Of course, it was living people who
prepared the dead and readied them for
burial.

The stories of the gods gave meaning to
that work.

Human hands and divine protection:
together, they shaped the funerary rites.

The idea of protection appears beyond
statues of the god, too.

The ritual object called an imiut combines
a staff, a jar, and a form wrapped in an
animal skin.

According to the museum, objects like this
and guardian figures were connected to
sacred spaces and funerary rites.
Protecting the dead took many forms.

Now we move from preparing the body to the
story of the journey after death.
Here we meet the Book of the Dead.

The museum notes that its ancient name was
the Book of Going Forth by Day.

It is a collection of spells and images on
papyrus, meant to help the deceased on
their way.

On screen now is a papyrus that
accompanied the burial of a woman named
Nauny.
The museum dates it to around 1050 BCE.

The scroll holds images and texts for
several spells, and among them is the
scene of the weighing of the heart.

It was made not for an abstract dead
person, but for one particular individual.
Why the heart?

Writing about another funerary papyrus,
the museum explains that the heart was

considered the center of intellect and
emotion.

In the weighing scene, how a person had
lived is what is being tested.

The heart was shown not as a mere organ,
but as a record of a life.

On the other side of the scale is
something representing Maat.

Maat is linked to order and to what is
right.

Many people picture only a feather, but in
Nauny's papyrus, Maat appears as a small
goddess wearing a feather.

It is worth remembering that one famous
image does not fit every source.

Here is another scene of Anubis and the
scale.

But this image is not a photograph of the
ancient wall painting itself.

It is a copy on paper, made by Nina de
Garis Davies from the tomb of Nakhtamun.

It is a valuable way to study the imagery,
but we present the original and the copy
as different things.
Let's look again at Nauny's papyrus.
Anubis is reading the scale.
But he is not alone in the scene.

There is a god who records the result, and
a god who receives the dead.

Once we separate these roles, the idea of
Anubis as a judge who decides everything
on his own turns out to be too simple.

On this fragment of cartonnage, Thoth,
with the head of an ibis, holds writing
equipment.

The museum describes the scene as Thoth
introducing the deceased to Osiris.

The clue to identifying a god is not just
the shape of the head.

What the god holds, and what the god is
doing, matter just as much.

According to the museum, if the scale
balanced, the deceased was accepted by
Osiris and granted eternal life.

If not, the heart was devoured by a
creature called Ammut, and the person died
forever.

Anubis weighs, Thoth records, Osiris
receives.

Judgment was pictured as a scene involving
many gods.

The judgment scene does have its
frightening side.

But the sources prepared for the dead were
not about failure alone.

They were about passing the test safely
and moving on to the next existence.

Seen through his role as a protector, the
same scene of the scale begins to look a
little different.

Now for a somewhat unexpected object: a
relief showing King Amenemhat I.

On either side of the king stand Horus and
Anubis, offering him the ankh, the sign of
life.

The museum connects this scene to royal
ritual.

Anubis appears in more places than the
weighing of the heart.

Here the king demonstrates, through
ritual, that even after a long reign he
still has the power to rule.

Anubis was connected to this place in his
role as lord of the necropolis.
The relief dates to around 1980 BCE.

Set beside later statues, it shows how the
same god was spoken of across a very long
span of time.

Much later, Anubis also appears on a
fragment of cartonnage from the Roman
period.

Osiris sits at the center, with Thoth and
other gods nearby.

Long after, the relationship between the
dead and the gods was still being
depicted.

Still, we need not treat each object as a
copy of exactly the same story.

For this small gold figure, the museum
offers two readings: it may be Anubis, or
it may be another god.

The museum states clearly that its
identity is uncertain.

Leaving the unknown as unknown is part of
telling history honestly.

A sharp image does not make an explanation
certain.

Beyond large paintings and statues, there
is also a figure of Anubis only about 7.7

centimeters tall, made of bronze or copper
alloy.

Exploring museum collections shows that
grand myths were also expressed in objects
small enough to hold in your hand.
Who used it, where, and how?
Small objects open up new questions.

Anubis was shown watching over tombs, took
part in the rites that prepared the body,
and appears in the weighing of the heart.

He is a god deeply bound to death, but his
role cannot be summed up by fear alone.

Protecting, and helping the dead pass
their test: the sources let us read him as
a god involved in both.

From the story of the heart preserved on
papyrus, we can take away a question.

If you could carry something beyond death,
what part of you would say who you were?

Behind the images of the gods, we can see
people's wish to support the dead on their
journey.
